utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor against Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before we go on with the witness, there are a number of things which I think have some urgency to dispose of. I'm sorry, sir. If you could just wait a few moments. A few things have blown up since you've been away. Mr. Bakrac, there are applications for protective measures for Witnesses 69, 89, and the third witness whom the Prosecution want to call, 249. Have you got any objection to those applications?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. I mean, nothing in addition to what has been said already on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's taken as agreed. Yes. Thank you very much indeed. Well, then, those applications in relation to 69, 89, and the witness to be known as 249 for protective measures sought will be granted. Now, there is a problem with the Sarajevo videolink date. We're told by the Registry that the shortage of staff, because they're working on some other videolinks at that time, that date is impossible. It certainly shows you that we're here in Holland when you get that answer, that it is not possible. Is there any particular reason why it has to be the 21st of March?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that somebody from the Prosecution speak to the people who actually arrange these things, find out which is the best day, and if you can get an agreement with them as to when you can get the Sarajevo videolink up and running - that was for 137 - we will make the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is for 137 and 49. There are two, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're quite right, yes. All right. Then we'll deal with those as soon as you can find out a date. Well, sir, we can come back to your evidence. You are still bound by the solemn declaration you took when you were here on the former occasion. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zekovic. Over the break we were able to obtain a transcript of your prior testimony, and I have a few questions to ask to clarify some things that you testified to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'll give the transcript page reference for the benefit of the Court and counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On page 3499 of the transcript, you testified that Juso Dzamalija killed himself in the KP Dom. Do you know how he was identified, that is, how his body was identified?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some kind of commission came in. There was some kind of doctor there, some kind of medical staff, and that they certified that he was dead. We heard that from the windows, as they were talking downstairs. He had hanged himself. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know why he hanged himself? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only make assumptions. I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty. I think that the man simply could not take all the torture that he was subjected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what torture specifically he was subjected to?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they beat him several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, on page 3439 you stated that before you were arrested and taken to the KP Dom, there was a time when you and other Muslim neighbours were rounded up in a cellar, and at that time some Serbian soldiers, according to your words, wanted to kill a Muslim neighbour who had a mental problem. And you testified, "But they did not. Not then." Can you tell us what happened to that neighbour who had the mental problems? Did something happen to him later?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He remained in that street for a long time. The last persons from my street were among the last people to be expelled from town in general. That was in August 1992. They were transferred on buses to Montenegro. That was when he was transferred as well. I don't know what happened to him afterwards, though. However, my street, our street, was among the last to be cleansed, ethnically cleansed in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And was that the time when your family was also expelled?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On page 3490 you described how a group of skilled metal shop workers were taken from the KP Dom in the late summer of 1992, and that Relja complained about this group of his workers being taken. You mentioned three names: Suad Islambasic, Abdulah Kameric, and Uzier -- Hadzalic, sorry, and Uzeir Hadzalic. Do you remember how many people were in that group who were taken out?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another one, Ismet Karahasanovic, and there was yet another one. But I don't know, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know how they were taken out?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how they were taken out. When they left, I was outside the working place. I was sent out to do some work, so I did not see how it all actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Of the men --

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one thing I do know, though. Uzeir Hadzalic was told by them on several occasions that he would be released because he was over 60 years old, and allegedly, according to some kind of law, such persons would be released. However, he was taken away and nothing has been heard about him since, or anybody from that group, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On page 3570 you testified that the guards who helped detainees were sent away from work. What do you mean by "sent away from work"? What happened to those guards?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sent to other working places, far more difficult ones or, rather, far more dangerous ones. People who tried in some way to help us -- I mean, these were very small things. Somebody would either bring tobacco, cigarettes, or a shaver or something like that, or messages from that person's family, whatever. However, if that were found out, then this was punished rigorously. Many asked me not to mention their names, as a matter of fact, because they could have problems. One of them told me directly that once he was released I should never mention his name, not to thank him in that way. However, the time will come when you will be able to do that, but not now, not for the time being. Do you understand that? I cannot give you their names. They still can have problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know who sent these guards away or who punished them for doing nice things for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the administration, nobody else could have done it. I mentioned already Milomir Maric, nicknamed Mara, one of the guards. He came to the isolation cell after my attempted escape. He came there and he threatened me. However, actually, he never did anything bad to anyone. He was just acting on the spur of the moment, but he didn't really mean it. Very often people would address him with various requests, to go to have lunch again or to get an extra slice of bread. And he asked people not to address him, not to talk to him, because he had terrible problems with the administration on account of that. In a way, he was a communicative person, a tolerant person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On the other side, what happened to the guards who beat and abused detainees? Were they ever punished?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of anyone ever being punished or sent away on account of that, no, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On page 3606, you described how when you began working in the coal mine in the spring of 1994, you had a knee injury, and you stated that a lady doctor used to come from the health centre. Did this doctor come from the health centre to the KP Dom during your entire time of detention or only, let's say, beginning the spring of 1994?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, that lady doctor came at that time. However, different doctors came to the KP Dom. First there was a doctor who escaped from Foca in August 1992. I personally know him. After that, there were periods when no doctor would come for a while. Otherwise, doctors would come twice a week. In the room there were 70 or 80 of us, and only five men could report for medical examinations or whoever would be appointed by the guards. Also, there were periods when no one would come. Also, there were periods when other doctors worked. I remember very well that once when I went to the metalwork shop, when I went out to work, on my way out, in that hall a doctor was speaking out loud, protesting, because he had been sort of reprimanded by the administration of the KP Dom because he had given some kind of sick leave to some of the prisoners in the KP Dom. He was hollering and he was upset. He said, "Nobody is going to interfere in my work. I know who is sick and I know who is not sick. If somebody is going to tell me what I'm supposed to do, I'm not going to come here to work any more." Of course I know this doctor's name, but I don't want to mention it now and I don't think it's important, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What time period was that? Do you remember what year? During the beginning or toward the end of your detention?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not at the beginning. Possibly this could have been the winter/spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you described a doctor who you said escaped from Foca in August 1992. Was that a Muslim doctor or Serb doctor?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Serb doctor. When he saw what had been done, when he viewed everything, he ran away. And he was a personal friend of mine, too. He tried to do something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say he tried to do something, do you mean he tried to do something to help the detainees?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, them and me. However, from the very moment he came to the KP Dom, there were always one or two guards with him. So he was not on his own for a single moment. In the summer of 1993, when he left, when he came to work the last time, he entered the metalwork shop, although that was not allowed. He saw me there. We chatted for a few minutes, and he never reappeared. He did not tell me then that he would be leaving. However, I found out seven or ten days later. Since he was not coming in for work, I asked what had happened to him. After that, I also went to the hospital once, and I knew some people there as well, so I would get medication from them every now and then. It's not that I needed medication that much, but there were people who were very ill, and that's how I found out that he had escaped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So was the year 1992 or 1993 when that doctor escaped? At one point you said 1992 and then it was 1993.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. 1992, that's right. August, mid-August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you said you would get medicine for people from the health centre, was that officially allowed?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not from the health centre. It was from the hospital, from the general hospital. No, absolutely this was not allowed, none of this. I tried to hide these medicines as I was bringing in my tool box. Then I would bring them into the room and give them to other men whenever I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, in your testimony, at one point you talked about --

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something else I wanted to tell you in connection with these medicines. On one occasion, a member of the medical staff at the hospital gave me medicine for Dr. Aziz Torlak. This was in the summer of 1992 -- no, 1993, before Dr. Torlak was taken away from the KP Dom and before I escaped. He gave me -- I can't tell you for sure now. He gave me some of his medicines and some of his things, and I brought this in. I hid it and then I tried to smuggle it to him, like a shaving kit too and all that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. However, after that he was taken in an unknown direction and nothing was ever heard of him since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, you testified at one point how you and other people in the metal shop made furnaces for the military and that you could have made furnaces for the detainees to keep warm, but you were not allowed to. I don't want to get into too much detail about the living conditions because other people have testified about that, but I would like to put this question to you: If someone were to suggest to you that living conditions were bad for everybody because of the wartime conditions, not just for the Muslim detainees, what would be your response to that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that. This is absolutely incorrect. It did not require any resources, any investment, or I don't know what, any kind of additional expenditures or extra work or whatever. It was very easy to do that. However, what you said just now could only be used as a pretext. If furnaces could not be given and if there wasn't enough firewood and coal, we could have got an extra blanket or extra clothes because there was plenty of that in the warehouses. However, even when the winter was at its coldest, you know that people had -- some people had three blankets or extra things, and all of that was taken away from them. Many windows were broken so it was terribly cold. It was more than terrible: It was really awful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, if somebody were to put to you that the KP Dom was divided into two different parts that were administered separately, and that Milorad Krnojelac was only in charge of the economic part and therefore not responsible for anything except the economic part, what would you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On what do you base that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base that on everything I know and all the time I spent there, everything I saw and heard. It is true that there was a division where Serbs were imprisoned for a week or several weeks, a month, longer than that; however, they were strictly separated from us. They had their own guards, their own supervisors. And collectively, the administration was one for the entire KP Dom. Perhaps there was some kind of a person who was in charge of the farm where the cows and the chickens were, a person in charge of agriculture. However, as to where we were, there was only one administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And was that the administration that Milorad Krnojelac was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, I would like to ask you about your brother, Enes Zekovic. You testified on page 3438 that he was arrested in mid-April of 1992 and detained at the KP Dom for two to two and a half months. When you were at the KP Dom, did you have contact with your brother? Did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had contacts. It so happened that our rooms were nearby at a corner. We could even talk because this was a three-metre distance. During the night we would establish contact, we would talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know if your brother was ever beaten at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about him ever being beaten, nor did he ever tell me any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know any particular reason why he was not beaten?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Even before you were taken to the KP Dom on the 20th of May, 1992, do you know if there were efforts on behalf of your brother to have him released from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were big interventions for him to be released. However, I know one thing for sure. One of the persons who was in charge there - I don't know any names right now - was opposed to that because the persons who had intervened on his behalf somehow were not on very good terms with this person. And then that person said, "Ah, now that such and such a person is intervening on his behalf, he is not going to be released." However, there were interventions coming in, even from the outside, even from Belgrade, and this ultimately resulted in his release.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- first of all, what is your brother -- or at that time, what was your brother's profession? At one point you mentioned that you had a brother who was a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked in the municipality as a clerk. This was the public attorney's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know whether Enes Zekovic's wife called Zdravko Begovic in an attempt to get her husband's released?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what was relayed back to her?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions I tried to talk to them about all of this; however, they are trying to keep their distance in that sense. They are terribly afraid. They keep silent about this. Even after my first testimony here, not only my brother but some other people warned me, in a way, that everything I said here could be very dangerous for me. However, I am not afraid. I think that these times are behind us, and that is my claim for several reasons. First of all, I will now certainly know how to defend myself and all of my own. Secondly, all of this cannot go by unpunished now. Now everybody knows that everybody will be held accountable for whatever they've done. Nevertheless, I think that there still are fanatical people who think and say that the war is not over yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, at one point in your prior testimony you described at page 3535 how Serb soldiers had hung metal rings from hand-grenades on the ears of one of the detainees who was taken as a kind of mine detector, and you said that this was used as a form of humiliation. Were there other acts of -- that appeared to you to be aimed at humiliating the Muslim detainees? Can you give us some examples, if any?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is what I did say about that man. That is Omer Bavcic from Gorazde. He was in isolation cell number four on the upper side, so to speak. And on one occasion when our meals were being given to us, we would go to the door and we would take our meals, and I saw that his ear was badly swollen and infected, even. And Predo Stefanovic, one of the guards, asked me, "What happened to you, big guy?" And he said, "I was out there with your men and we were working with mines, doing something with mines, and that's what happened." And I know of another case. I was not there personally, but I heard this from all the people who were up there at the farm. Jasarevic, I cannot remember his first name, worked up there with a group of men near a motel called Brioni. They were building a wire bridge. They were actually oiling the wood in order to protect it. Zelja came there, Zelenovic. He came there with some friends of his. At one moment he called out Atif Jasarevic's name. And this man came up to him, and he took a brush and this oil - this oil was all black because it was old oil that had already been used in machines, lubricating oil - and then he put it on his face and he said, "See? It is such people who are protecting you." He was probably alluding to Arabs. It was unbelievable how susceptible they all were to the media propaganda. The unbelievable things that they were being told they accepted without resorting to common sense at all. Once, in the summer of 1992, Milenko Burilo, Busi, was a guard within the metalwork shop where we were working, and at one moment he started talking, and he said that everything that was being done to us was nothing compared to what Alija Izetbegovic was doing in Sarajevo. He said that he got lions from Libya and that he was throwing Serb children to the lions in Sarajevo. And in order to make the story complete, he said that this was also being done by Josip Pejakovic, a well-known actor who had not joined the SDS and who did not join the army. At that moment, I and that friend of mine who has the code name 210 here --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We are getting a little bit off the subject. When the guards -- I'm sorry. When Zelja and his men put the grease on the face of the detainee, did any of the KP Dom guards intervene?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, did you ever try to record your experiences by writing them down after your release?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did make some efforts. However, a friend of mine who is engaged in publishing was talking me into it. But every time I tried, I would give up the moment I started, and I sort of put it off. More subconsciously than consciously I didn't want to do that because that brought it all back and I had to go through it all over again and that isn't easy at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Perhaps this isn't easy either, but can you tell us how you are still psychologically affected by your experience in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not easy to describe or to explain. Very often I cannot sleep at night. It takes me a long time to get to sleep. The dreams I dream are terrible. I wake up in a sweat, in fear. I dream of all sorts of escape. I am trying desperately to escape, to reach that light that's waiting afar, and every time they catch up with me and start beating me again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. Those are all the Prosecution's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, before we have the cross-examination, there is that issue about the translation of this witness's evidence on the last occasion. The case is going to be raised in cross-examination, so we have got to sort it out now. At the end of the last day, that was the 22nd of February, I asked the Languages Section to check the translation of the passage which now appears at page 3580, at lines 6 to 9, and I suggested it might be best if a number of different interpreters could listen to the tape independently to see whether this hotly disputed passage was correctly interpreted. Now, I don't know whether that has been done. Has the Prosecution heard anything of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We didn't think that they would submit it to us but, rather, directly to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've heard nothing. Have you heard anything, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I wonder if somebody could let us know, perhaps after the short adjournment, whether that has been checked. It was the passage in the LiveNote record, page 75, lines 21 to 24, and they have now been reproduced, I haven't checked them against the original LiveNote at 3580, lines 6 to 9. Is this your cross-examination, Mr. Vasic? Well, if you do intend to ask any questions about that, I suggest you wait until we've had that checked, to see whether it has been checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zekovic. I should like to introduce myself. I am lawyer Miroslav Vasic, one of the defenders of the accused Milorad Krnojelac. My first question would relate to the statements you have given to the investigators of the Prosecutor's office. Do you recall a statement given on the 5th, 6th, and 7th of May, 1999? We didn't hear your voice.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you also give a statement to the Ministry of the Interior, the public security centre, the state security service in Sarajevo on the 14th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would appreciate it very much if you could pause before answering for the sake of the interpreters and so that the Chamber and my colleagues from the Prosecution office know what my question was. Do you know if the state security service in Sarajevo is also known under the name of AID?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt that perhaps two years ago, but I don't see that it matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A question arose here, and it was also a matter of concern for the Trial Chamber, what AID meant, and I'm trying to clarify that. Did you talk to members of this agency, AID?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As was mentioned then, it was the so-called DB, the state security, the state security centre. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mean this conversation, this interview in 1994?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that interview, did you have another contact with members of this agency?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In response to the question of my learned friend, you have mentioned that you saw in the KP Dom Sain, Bozo, as a commander of a unit which laid mines. Is that correct? Was that the first time that you saw Bozo Sain since the beginning of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that Muslim units shelled Serbian positions from the beginning of the armed conflict from a position known as Sukovac?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were in Sukovac, and the Serbs were in Cerezluk and up there in Zabrana.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you state to the state security service that you had met Bozo Sain before you were arrested and that he had shown you a big heap of unexploded shells, and that he told you that those shells had been fired from Sukovac but failed to explode because the safety catches, or whatever it's called, were not removed from them?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So your previous answer is not correct, the one when you said that you first saw Bozo Sain in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had forgotten all about it. That happened a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you saw Bozo Sain in the KP Dom, was he wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was anybody else present during your brief interview?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We just exchanged a couple of words in passing when we were on our way to breakfast. It was just a moment, ten or 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me, please, why this event, this incident, related to the conversation with Bozo Sain in the KP Dom has never been mentioned by you in any interview, either with the security centre or with the representatives of the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot remember all events at any single moment. If I went through this whole story again, I could possibly remember many more things that I have experienced and that I had learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would agree, but in your statement to the security centre you mentioned Bozo Sain's name. Didn't you have any associations once you mentioned it with other incidents when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement which I gave to the CSB, I did not cover even 50 per cent of the -- of what I said here. It was not a detailed conversation; it was a general outline. And it is absolutely certain that I failed to mention a great number of things because nobody asked me question details, detailed enough. I couldn't even remember everything at the time, and they were not interested in such great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Don't you think that the security centre was more interested in details about who ordered the mining of the KP Dom compound than your meeting with Bozo Sain who showed you the shells of the grenades?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why they should be interested whether the KP Dom was mined from the inside or that Maglic was mined on the outside border.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the name of Suljo Hasanbegovic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us to which party he belonged?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think he was affiliated to the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he a representative of the SDA for Foca?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you could call him that. I think that's the way you can put it, although I had no contact with him. I was -- I had an argument with him. I had a quarrel with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What kind of quarrel?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a job to do together involving an investment abroad. There were problems and we ultimately had to deal with that in court. It was some kind of joint venture, and we had a disagreement about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what year that was?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That disagreement with Mr. Hasanbegovic and the lawsuit, the trial.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- well, I don't know exactly. 1990 or 1989, perhaps. For the life of me, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mean before the armed conflict, before the military operations?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you give a statement to the security centre saying that Suljo Hasanbegovic had given you a rifle which you had hidden?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When did Mr. Hasanbegovic give you that rifle?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't give it directly to me. He sent a young man to bring the rifle to me. It was a couple of months before the beginning of the war. I disassembled the rifle, and I threw it away. I didn't even bury it; I threw it away into the so-called caves on the bank of the Drina River. But if I had been wiser, I wouldn't have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why did he send the rifle to you?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I wouldn't have disassembled it and thrown it away if I had known what was in the works. What do you mean, that I don't have a right to defend myself? We all believed that it wouldn't happen. I mean, the overwhelming majority of us didn't believe that it would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but why did he send you the rifle? That's the question you didn't answer.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To defend myself. And as you are aware, we failed to do that in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, about anything that was found during the search of Suljo Hasanbegovic's house, if anything?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were rumours, there were stories circulating, but I was really not interested. All I know is that he escaped. I know that his father-in-law had some problems because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, did you give a statement to the state security centre saying that some automatic rifles and uniforms were found in Suljo Hasanbegovic's house?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I said that, in those words at least. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you go on to say that fortunately he destroyed the lists according to which he distributed weapons?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would it help you if I were to show you a copy of that statement where at the bottom of the page you signed your name, Ekrem Zekovic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that I didn't. I don't remember all the details. I know that he had something, but I never had any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Were you a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify for us what it means, "in a way"?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not a fervent supporter, but I did vote for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you, as a member of the SDA, receive a rifle from Mr. Hasanbegovic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't go along those lines. It didn't matter whether somebody was a member of the SDA or not. Sometimes such things were sold for money. Sometimes they were procured in a different way. What mattered is who needed it. And I was naive. I didn't believe that anything would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hasanbegovic distribute weapons to Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't, no, but I know of others who did. They made a business out of it. They sold weapons. They traded weapons. Speculation and contraband was a great opportunity for making profit. As we say where I come from, it's a good time for bad people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: From what time were you a member of the SDA, from what year?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I can call myself a member at all in any terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you have a membership card?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never got one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you pay any membership fees?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you state to members of the state security service that your investigation in the KP Dom took about half an hour because the investigators did not know whether you were a member of the SDA or that you possessed weapons?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I don't know if it took 30 minutes. Perhaps 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you were a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does it matter? Was I a criminal if I was a member of the SDA? Did I do anything bad to anyone? Did I kill anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying you did, sir.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I didn't say you killed anyone. I just asked whether you were a member of the SDA and whether it was on account of that that you procured weapons.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should have been wiser. I should have procured weapons to defend myself of my own accord. If I had been a member of the SDA, that doesn't mean that I was a criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Zekovic, I realise that you have an emotional reaction to the question, but you really must wait for a significant time after the question before you start to answer it so that the translators can catch up. Mr. Vasic, do you think that we may have spent enough time on this? He has said that he supported the SDA. He was more or less a member of the SDA. If there is some little statement that he has made that he was a member of the SDA, I don't think it is going to be anything in conflict with what he's given in evidence about here, and if that's the only matter that you want to deal with, let's move on to something more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It was just a small test of credibility. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, Suljo could have put me on the list to have a certain number of people on the list. They used to do that. They put people on the list who were not fit to serve in the army, for no reason, or somebody could simply boast of having a lot of activists on their list, and it's possible that Suljo, for a reason like that, added me to his list, but I never had coffee with him even, let alone something more meaningful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, you may rest assured that we are not very concerned about whether you were or you were not a member of the SDA. The issue has been dealt with. Let's get on with something that is relevant in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, are you aware that during -- while the war was on, for a while the Green Beret forces held the KP Dom in Foca?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did -- as a result of the combat activities that were going on at that time, was the KP Dom damaged?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't say that. I don't think that anything was damaged or looted. So you are calling them Green Berets. That is fine if you're calling them that way, but when they came in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us today that the windows, the glass in the windows in the KP Dom were broken. How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why they were broken. Some windows could not be closed tightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: One thing is -- are the windows that could not close tightly and quite a different matter are the broken windows.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you are looking for. I don't know whether there was any combat going on at that time because I was not in town at the time. The KP Dom was operational when it was taken over. Now, whether there was a glass, a window that was broken, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now you've just told us that you were not in that part of the town so that you don't know about this, and this is an answer that I would agree with. But prior to that, you told us that the KP Dom was not damaged, was not destroyed. How could you know that if you were not present in that part of the town?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was overhearing once -- when I was going to work, I was listening to a conversation in a cafe, and I heard that there were three or four break-ins. I heard a conversation when Mitar Rasevic said this, and the others responded, "Well, it was Muslims that looted and took everything away." And Mitar Rasevic responded, "No, that is not true. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. When we came in and took over the KP Dom, every lock was operational. Some weapons were missing, some Italian rifles. However, that was later found in some kind of a ditch."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that a former warden of the KP Dom, once the war broke out, ordered the safety valves to be taken off the weapons and thrown away?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. People who used to work there would know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rasevic, in the conversation that you just described to us, did not mention that, did he?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. There was no mention of rifles or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Are you aware whether the SDA party had a Crisis Staff in Foca and who was the chairman of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know who was the chairman of that Crisis Staff. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, sir, take the soldiers to the apartment of Mehmedspahic, Nijaz?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of a formation called White Eagles or something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what Zelovic, Dragan told the members of that formation, the White Guard?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told them not to loot, that this was the agreement they had reached. He simply said, "Don't touch anything. They is what we have agreed on," and that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your statement in front of the Trial Chamber you mentioned a Serbian guardsman who came to your house frequently and what he said on the occasion when he visited your house. Why didn't you mention this member of the guard formation in any of your previous statements?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you previously, if we were to carry this conversation for long enough, I would remember a number of things. And this member of the guard formation is hopefully alive and well in Serbia. And all of those who committed evil things will have to be held accountable before a court or before God. And if I am able, I will repay in kind to this man. My wife -- he would come every day, and he threatened everybody that -- he threatened everybody not -- not to touch any of the Serb people who were living there; otherwise, he would kill them all. And he said once, "It is true that I am a Serb. It is true that I am a Chetnik, but I'm not the same as those -- as the others. I'm from Sumadija, and we're simply interested in having a good time and singing." And then my wife and the others who were there, they asked him, "Well, why did you come here?" and he replied, "Well, we came here because we were told that there was a massacre going on here, that 500 Serbs had been killed, and this is why we came here. And when we came, we realised that it is not so." Later on this Serb, this man, took my wife in his car to see her parents in a different village. And after that, one of their members was killed in the school centre, and after that they went back to Serbia. And before he went back, he came to say good-bye to my wife and to my family, and I can provide further evidence to this. And before he left, he said, "May God help you because these other Serbs here are just very evil." And as we know, there was no massacre of Serbs in Foca. We know very well where massacres took place and who was massacred. While Muslims held the KP Dom, nobody was killed there. There were some people who were locked up there, that's what I heard, but I don't know of anyone who was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Visegrad, Gorazde, Foca. Could the same be applied to Zenica, Sarajevo, Celebici? Do you have knowledge about these places as well?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a public -- this is a matter of public knowledge. This has been printed in the media and everywhere, and now all that needs to be done is to shed light on this. But there are -- there is information to this effect. On one day in December of 1992, Mitar Rasevic told me as I was telling him, "Well, why is this going on? I never did anything bad to anyone." And he replied to me, "Yes, yes, I know that. But none of this would be taking place if it wasn't for the operation which took place on the 9th of May when the JNA was retreating from its barracks and a number of people were killed on that occasion in Skenderija in Sarajevo." And that took place sometime in May, but however, the entire eastern part of Bosnia was set on fire prior to that and a great number of people were killed as well. However, he told me that nothing would have come about if it weren't for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that answer, which was a very long one, was really provoked by what seems to be an inescapable tactic which has been raised in so many of these cases. We are not concerned here with what happened, for example, in Celebici. I mean, we know what happened in Celebici, and we know that Serbs were badly treated there, but we are not concerned with what happened to the Serbs in this case. We are concerned with whether or not there was an attack upon the civilian population of the Muslims. And the fact that there was no doubt an attack upon the civilian population of the Serbs elsewhere in the country has nothing to do with it. Now, any question that you ask, and it is a question which keeps on coming up even in this case, is going to provoke answers like that. And it seems to me that we are wasting so much time. This Tribunal has had to try cases where Serbs were the victims, so we know that they were victims during the course of this armed conflict. But we're not concerned with it in this case because the fact that there was an attack upon the Serb population somewhere else does not mean, or even within Foca, does not mean that there was not also an attack upon the civilian population of the Muslims. So let's get on with the real issues in this case. We are not concerned with who started the war, why it was started, or who was at fault in relation to the war. We are only concerned with the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you in your statement given to the security centre, did you state there that those who failed to respond to mobilisation in Foca faced confiscation of all of their real property and moveable property, also faced being proclaimed traitors and deported from that region?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you in your statement given to the security service centre say that Todovic, Savo was in charge of the treatment of imprisoned Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I repeated that on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Boro Ivanovic was on behalf of military command in charge of the treatment of Muslims in the KP Dom. Did he tell you this personally?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Boro was there very frequently, and I was able to see that after my escape as well. He and Savo Todovic went together to Montenegro to wait for me there, and then they interrogated me together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you hear personally ever that Boro Ivanovic issued orders to Milorad Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not able to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we then believe that your statement to this effect is your own conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a known fact based on the conversations with other people, with guards. We knew who held what positions and who was what.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if that is indeed so, why then Milorad Krnojelac did not go with Boro Ivanovic to ambush you? Why did he take Savo Todovic with him?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't see what would be the point of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you reply to my question?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why didn't Milorad Krnojelac go to ambush me? Because he was the warden. He probably had more important things to do. How would I know why he didn't go?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who told you that Milorad Krnojelac was subordinated to Boro Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on their relationship and based on what I heard when talking to various guards, we were able to find out who held what positions. Also, based on our contacts with various Serbs in town, we could find this out. Boro didn't come to me to say that he was the boss of Krnojelac and Todovic. That certainly didn't happen that way, and I wasn't in a position to go and verify this. However, those were the ones who knew everything and who were in the position to do either positive or negative things. I recently -- I also talked to a man who a few days ago had talked to Boro Ivanovic and who apparently claims that he knows nothing and had not done anything, and the people then told me, "Well, if you are not guilty, why do you go to all this trouble to defend yourself? And if you are indeed guilty, then you will go to a place where you deserve to go." Boro Ivanovic says that everything that took place there is something that the KP Dom administration should be aware of. And now the municipality is building him a house, I guess for all the good things that he had done in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on your response, you concluded, based on what you heard, that Milorad Krnojelac was subordinated to Boro Ivanovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Ivanovic was in higher command bodies than are wardens.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you state to the OTP investigators that the widespread arrests of Muslims started between the 20th and the 25th of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. As of May 15th, people were released from the -- certain people were released from the KP Dom and also the visits were allowed. After that, it was very rare that they allowed visits. Only few people managed to get that approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether during your stay at the KP Dom -- can you tell us, during your stay there in which rooms you lived and at which time?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can do that. I first stayed in Room 18, and then a room was established for those who worked together, Room 22 and Room 16. Then later on in the fall when there were fewer of us, we were transferred to the old wing of the house, in Room 13. I cannot remember exactly now. I don't see how this is relevant. I lived in many rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It is important because of the events and the individuals you are mentioning. When you say "the fall," do you mean the fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Room 13. Yes, that was the fall of 1993, the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state to the state security centre that a number of prisoners who were believed to be SDA activists and when possessed arms were taken to the isolation cells and beaten? When asked by my learned friend, you said that people were taken out randomly. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but the answer to the previous question was not recorded in the transcript. The witness replied "yes," and this is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I must say I didn't hear him say anything. You heard him say "yes"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard, but let me ask the question again and give the witness a chance to reply once again. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you state to the state security centre employees that certain prisoners who were believed to be SDA activists and who were believed to possess weapons were taken to the isolation cells and beaten?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. However, that was not the only criteria. All of us were considered suspects, even those who before the war went to Serbia, Montenegro. They were considered suspects as well, and those who surrendered to the JNA as well. So all of us were suspected of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So there was a criteria based on this suspicion to establish who played what role? Can you please reply more loudly because your answer was not recorded. So was there a criteria to establish who played which role? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how would I know what were their criteria? No Muslim or Croat was considered to be clear or good. We were all either imprisoned or deported from Foca. A friend of mine whose wife is a Serb, she left prior to the war to Serbia, and he remained there because he had his job there. They asked him ten times, "Well, why did you remain here?" He was not a member of the SDA. All he knew was that he wanted to drink and to work. And they asked him a number of times why his wife had left to Serbia, to go to her family. Therefore, he was considered guilty because his wife left for Serbia and he remained there, and they would also suspect him of various things if he had not left himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony here before this Trial Chamber that Mr. Balic was beaten in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you say to the members of the state security service that he was beaten because he was a member of the SDA and had weapons?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're going back to the same issue. He was beaten mostly because his brother, Husein Balic, was the director or he was the principal of the military school in Vranica and he gave certain statements, and I guess the members of that school were taken hostage. After his brother was released, he gave a certain statement and then his brother, Dzemo, was prosecuted. However, they attributed various things to us. They would, for example, ask us whether we had Croatian money, whether we had Croatian flags. And what use would we have for Croatian money in Foca? They searched my apartment to see if I had any Croatian currency. So they simply used anything as a pretext. They had no specific proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now, did you in fact state what I had told you, that he was beaten because he was a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they beat him because they wanted to see whether he had lists and whether he was the organiser of this group. However, if he indeed had been, then they would have been able to prove that. However, they weren't able to prove anything. If we were truly organised, then there wouldn't be as many of us in the KP Dom and other camps. One guy was beaten because they wanted him to admit that he was a member of the SDA. I know this for a fact because I heard this with my own ears, and this young man was quite desperate, and he was saying, "Well, I'm not a member. I'm not a member. Even my cow is not a member of the SDA; however, you killed my cow." Not everybody was a member of the SDA. And why was that relevant? We're going back to the same issue. Why is it important whether somebody was a member of the SDA or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned an incident with this young guy. When did this take place?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it. I heard them beat him and ask that he give a confession of being a SDA member.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now, which month was it in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I had already started working. It could have been August or September or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where were you when you heard that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in front of the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was it outside of the compound or in front of the metal gate?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was outside of the compound. I was repairing a vehicle right by the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And where was this young man at the time?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside one of the rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which room, which floor?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the ground floor. I'm not sure exactly which room it was, but it was on the ground floor. Perhaps it was the, what we call the passing room or the -- one of the isolation cells, the transit room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you mean this transit isolation cell that you mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is 11.00, so this is perhaps a convenient moment to stop the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll reconvene at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the delay. It was my fault. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break, we were talking about a young man. You said that you had heard that he had been beaten because he was a member of the SDA. Why did you not mention this to the investigator of the OTP when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to you a few minutes ago, there are lots of things that I have not said. I could not recall everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the OTP investigator ask you about details, about events that you were aware of, of which you had immediate knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he did. But as I said, there were lots of things that happened in those two and a half years in the camp that I heard, that I saw, that I found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you found out about this detail?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did I find out about this detail? I remembered just now, a few minutes ago when we were talking about whether I was a member of the SDA or whether somebody else was a member of the SDA, and I was saying that people were being accused or, rather, suspected of being something, only on the basis of that, and that's when I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that Mr. Balic was beaten up and that you had seen him after that.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why did you not mention this detail to the investigator of the OTP or to the state security centre? Did you remember this just before you testified about it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said that to the Prosecutor. I think that that had been mentioned. After Dzemo Balic got out of the isolation cell, he came to my room. When I was detained on the 20th of May, he was in the isolation cell. After a long time, he got out. The man was at his wits end. He could not talk to anyone for days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the investigator of the OTP, I did not come across this piece of information that you had said that, that is.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, you did not say what you stated before the Honourable Trial Chamber, that you saw Mr. Sahinovic, Mr. Rizvanovic in the transit isolation cell, beaten up, and that you talked to them.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who did I not say that to? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You did not say that to the investigator of the OTP. Those persons are not mentioned in your statement.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the statement I gave to the OTP two years ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Two years ago.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, because there are many things that I have not mentioned yet at all that we simply did not bring up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you say whether the detainees could move about the compound of the KP Dom without being escorted by guards?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Depends on what?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the work concerned, on the circumstances involved. There were some people who worked within the compound. They were cutting firewood or cleaning the compound, and usually they had guards accompanying them. We from the metalwork shop, when we came to do something within the compound of the camp itself, we did not have any special guards assigned to us, but there were guards that were within the compound. So we did not have a guard from the outside coming in to escort us while we were in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you then supervised by the guards who were in the compound of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you know that on the first floor in the administration building of the KP Dom there was a restaurant where coffee was prepared?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not on the first floor. It was on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to the one on the ground floor, was there that kind of restaurant on the first floor as well? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's question, you spoke of a conversation that you heard from the room on the ground floor that you mentioned just now. On that occasion, was the window open in that room?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in front of the metal gate on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we would wait for ten minutes and sometimes for an entire hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While you were waiting for ten minutes or for an entire hour, were you supervised by a guard?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Not even one from the compound of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These guards from the compound of the KP Dom were moving about the compound of the KP Dom. They were at every entrance into the building, in front of the kitchen. Also above the building of the KP Dom there were several of them. But whether there was someone who was specifically standing by us, next to us by the gate as we were standing there waiting to go out to work, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were allowed to get that close to the administration building? You were allowed to stand there and wait?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we weren't allowed, but we weren't forbidden, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you would sometimes wait for an hour or for ten minutes? What were you waiting for?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to come before 7.00, and we would wait for someone to come, one of the guards to come, for the head of the metalwork shop to come and to call us out and to take us out to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the guards work in three shifts? Was a guard always present at the metal gate on the inside?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the inside? There was not a guard on the inside. There was a guard in the reception office within the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So which guard did you wait for to take you to the metal shop?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who would be assigned that way to guard us, to guard us within the metal shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As for the details of the conversation that you heard through the window, did you talk to the investigator of the OTP about this and also to the people at the security centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course in Sarajevo I did not talk about such minor matters. They didn't ask me about that, either. They asked me approximately how many people were there and whether people were taken out and when they were taken out for these exchanges, and that all trace was lost of them. But whether I told them about these details, what I heard there and what I heard at the metalwork shop or by the wall, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you remember this detail just before you testified?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you state the following to the investigator of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I listened to these conversations, that I heard them; is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I cannot find that in your statement dated 1999, the one I got from the OTP. Do you think that it was simply not recorded, as insignificant?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it was not recorded at all. Possibly it was not recorded at all because I spoke about some things at great length and I went into great detail, and then they said that some things were not all that significant for the case involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you listened to the conversation that was taking place in the office by the metalwork shop. Were you alone then?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when I was eavesdropping in front of this office?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this happened, in which month, which year? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the summer of 1992, the autumn. Sometimes during the winter as well, because at first we did not have the key to this workshop. It is only later that a man was asked to work there as a locksmith, so then we had access to the room. At first we did not have access to that room at all, then Relja would give us the key from time to time. Sometimes this was once or twice a week and sometimes it was only once in 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While you testified in response to my learned friend's questions, you said that beatings could be heard every day.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, all the way up to - I don't know - September, something like that, almost every day. For example, there would be four or five days in succession and then there wouldn't be any in a few days. So these intervals were irregular, but at any rate, it was very frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why did you not mention this in the statements you made so far to the investigator of the OTP and also to the security station?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are going back to that again. The statement I made to the security station was very brief, and I did not include many things there. They did not ask me about a great many things and perhaps not everything was of interest to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It is a ten-page statement, the one that you gave to the security station, and the statement you gave to the investigator of the OTP is ten and a half pages. Do you think that in these ten pages not everything you said was included or did you simply not mention that then?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that not everything was included. It is also possible I did not mention some things to them. I repeat once again, there are many things that perhaps I did not mention at all to anyone yet, that we have not brought up yet. There are some that I mentioned for the first time today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is one of these things your statement relating today to what you know about the beating of the man from Kamena because of the water and what he heard? That is what you stated before the Honourable Trial Chamber in response to my learned friend's question.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before you did not mention this at all.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is the umpteenth time that I am saying this. I cannot remember all the details. I do not know exactly which are the details I did mention and which are the details I did not mention, but whatever I have said, I stand by it. I said some things in Sarajevo. I did not say a great many thing in Sarajevo. Some things I said to the investigators and there are other things that we did not pay any attention to. It was impossible for me to remember everything at a given point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the investigator of the OTP ask you about beatings of which you had immediate knowledge?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he did, but there were so many beatings that I could not remember everything. It's not that it was only a few incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement to the investigator of the OTP, you did not mention that many beatings. It's not that you could not have remembered something that you personally heard and saw and also concerning a person that was together with you in Room 18, as you've said.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand what you've been saying. What is this? Who is this person?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that this young man from Kamena was beaten because of water and that he was in Room 18 with you.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Room 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say that when you gave a statement to the investigator of the OTP, you did not remember this incident.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many things that I did not remember. I can remember them now when we are taking things in a certain order and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to my learned friend's question, you said that beatings took place behind the metal door in the anteroom and in other rooms that you could not locate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After that, you said that you saw blood on the walls and also the cash register behind the metal door.

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it wasn't a cash register. It was a metal cupboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Oh, a metal cupboard. Did you remember this detail just now, just before you testified?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always knew that. I passed through that metal gate hundreds of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why did you not say that to the investigator of the OTP then? Did you think that this was an insignificant detail?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you really must wait. Mr. Vasic, I know you're doing your best and usually you're successful, but you are coming in on top of his answers. Mr. Zekovic, it's very hard to understand this, I suppose. Everything that you are saying is being translated into English and into French. Now, that works very well when the counsel cross-examining you is speaking in a different language to yourself because there has got to be a pause while you listen for the translation before you give the answer. But because you can hear it coming in your language, you tend to come in too soon. So please just wait so that the interpreters have got the chance to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the first time that you mentioned blood on the walls and the metal wardrobe here in court. I'm just asking whether you remembered all of that just before you testified?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again: I remembered many details later when we get into these matters, when we start discussing them. I answered many direct questions before, and there are many things that I remembered and that I talked about. I was always aware of this information. I know that these walls were bloody, and I know that just before the Red Cross came to visit they were painted. And I know the people who did that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you are entitled to take everything that he has said here and point out to him that he has not referred to it in any statement that he signed, or he does not appear to have referred to.
