utterances.text: You were asked questions during cross-examination about this vehicle that you saw which had just been washed and you saw blood in the water, and there were some questions asked about the use of the vehicle at the fish farm. Is it possible that the blood you saw that day, that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. morning, came from fish blood?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know. Because every day before that I had been out in that yard, and that car was parked in the yard of the metalwork shop. And the atmosphere at the time, the prevailing situation was such that there was no question of going fishing, and the fishpond had been destroyed. There was no fish there any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about something brought up during cross-examination which is that you never mentioned what happened to Dzemo Balic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And if I could have the assistance of the usher in showing the witness what was marked for identification as ID 334, and it will be page 4, ten lines from the bottom in the B/C/S version. In the English version, which is ID 334A, it's at the top of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And this is a statement that you gave to the security services centre in Sarajevo in October 1994. I'll just read it to you and have you confirm whether you said this. It's ten lines from the bottom, sir. Did you tell the security forces at that time: "Likewise in the same period, a number of prisoners suspected of being SDA activists and of possessing weapons were taken to solitary confinement where they were beaten up. I know that Dzemo Balic spent 25 days in solitary confinement, but would not give away SDA members and other individuals who possessed weapons." Is that accurate? Is that what you told the state security centre in October 1994?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I said it in those words. Dzemo Balic told me before he was taken away, and he hadn't spoken to anyone for a long time before that, he said that he was beaten something horrible. They were forcing him to make a list of SDA members, lists of people who had weapons, some kind of lists of wartime assignments, and he couldn't do that because he didn't know anything of the kind. He just couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But you did say, you did mention in your statement in 1994 about what happened to Mr. Balic, right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving that evidence. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, according to the file, FWS-214 has no protective measures, or is it one of the ones we just dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he has requested nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, nevertheless we have prepared a sheet of people for this witness because he may refer to other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Have you got a document there?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P-436, and it will be under seal. Whilst we're waiting for the witness to arrive, we have another problem tomorrow afternoon. Judge Mumba and I are once again required for an administrative purpose. I hope it's the last of the interruptions of this trial, which are becoming somewhat tedious. We have to be at this meeting at 3.30. Now, it seems to me that we'll need some time to get there. If we sit through to 3.20, my question is whether we would be able to resume at 2.20 so at least we get an hour. That will require some consideration to be given by the interpreters and typists and those who have rather strict rules about breaks. When we resume after they've had a chance to consider the matter, they can let us know in the morning, but we will certainly be adjourning at 3.20 tomorrow afternoon. As I say, I hope it's the last of these interruptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration. It's set out in the document which is being shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down please, sir. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please state your name and your birth date?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: My name is Amir Berberkic. I was born on the 1st of January, 1958.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you yourself had not requested any protective measures, but other witnesses have done so. You find therefore in front of you a sheet of paper with many names and many witness numbers, so in case you want to refer to any of these witnesses listed here, please do not tell their name but just refer to the number on this sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I have understood what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I was born in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say Bosniak, do you mean a Muslim? Are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim by religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Are you married?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I am married, and I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I lived in the centre of town in a family home. The street of Marsala Tita, number 21.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was your profession before the war?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Before the war I was a physician. I worked at the emergency ward in the hospital in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, I do not want to discuss political background or tension in Foca. The only matters related to this, I would like to ask you about two of your colleagues. And first of all, I would like to know if you do know a Dr. Radovan Mandic?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Dr. Radovan Mandic personally because he worked at the hospital. He was head of the haemology department. I know him personally. I saw him a few times at the hospital. We attended physicians' meetings together and also at meetings that we held of the Association of Doctors of the Upper Drina Region, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Mandic, was he involved in politics especially? Was he an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He was involved in politics as far as I know. He was engaged in the so-called Focatrans affair which occurred two years before the war, I think. I even watched him on television once when he made a statement at the time. As far as I know, he was a member of the SDS, and I think - people talked about it at the hospital then - that at the beginning of the war he was president of the Crisis Staff of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Which people talked about his position in the Crisis Staff, Serbs or Muslims or both?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that both talked about it. Foca is a small town. You have to know that. Many things that happen in town and everything that has to do with the town itself is found out very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know which position he had in the -- you said already he was head of the Crisis Staff. Sorry. I also want to address another doctor, Dr. Kornjaca. Do you know this person, Dr. Kronjaca, from Cajnice?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I know Dr. Kornjaca personally. I talked to him a few times. He worked in Cajnice, at the hospital there. He stopped by very often at the regional centre, the hospital in Foca where I worked. About a year before the war broke out, he started wearing a camouflage uniform, which I found to be very strange. I did not understand why he wore a long beard too and a camouflage uniform, as I said, military boots as well, and also a small leather bag which was worn by commanders in the Second World War, something like that. Once in Gorazde, perhaps about a year before the war broke out, we had a meeting of the doctors' association. He appeared in camouflage uniform at that meeting. Of course, at that time I did not understand what this meant, what it was supposed to mean. I didn't pay much attention to it, but I really wondered why a camouflage uniform at a doctors' meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Dr. Kornjaca, is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: He's a Serb. Before the war, one morning in the newspaper Oslobodjenje, on the last page, I remember very well that I read that together with his brother and Dr. Miladin Lisov, who also worked at the Foca hospital, who is a colleague of mine, that he was singing Chetnik songs in the hotel in Cajnice. Of course, that morning as we were drinking coffee, Dr. Lisov was there and also Dr. Aziz Torlak. He was a surgeon who also worked at the hospital there. We were drinking coffee, and I was reading Oslobodjenje, on that last page I found that text. Of course I found it very strange, because Miladin Lisov was a participant. He sang these songs too. I remember which songs he sang that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. We do not need to go into more details on this matter. Thank you. Let's move on to April 1992 and the outbreak of the war in Foca. When the war broke out in Foca, did you go to work that day?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think it was Monday morning, the 7th of April. I had a car, a Yugo, a red one, and I set out to go to work as I did every day before that. However, I came across two roadblocks in the part of town that is called Donje Polje. I didn't realise what was going on at the time. I asked. These were people who belonged to the so-called Territorial Defence. They wore uniforms that the prewar police had worn. Most of these people were of Muslim ethnicity, and I asked them what was going on. I said I was supposed to go to work to the hospital. They said it was far too dangerous. They said they would let me through, but they could not give me any guarantees that I would arrive at the hospital alive because, as they had put it, the Chetniks started shooting from the hills surrounding the town at the town itself. I set out, and then in front of the KP Dom I saw a truck that was parked right in the middle of the road. I somehow managed to drive around this truck, and I managed to get to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I stayed at the hospital for about 12 days or perhaps two weeks, and I was present all the time until Foca fell. That was approximately the 20th of April. That's when I left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During this time at the hospital, did you prepare for emergencies?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: That morning, we held a meeting of doctors who worked at the surgery department, together with the head of surgery, Dr. Kosta Supic. The meeting was attended by Aziz Torlak, myself, and our Serb colleagues, doctors who happened to be working that morning. Our boss told us that our task was to stay in the hospital, that we would organise everything for the wounded, the wounded that would be coming in, as he had put it, and also we would allocate duty according to different days and that we would have a so-called emergency centre, a clinic where we would take in the wounded. He also said to us that it would be smart if we would bring the members of our families, our wives and children, to the hospital because the hospital was a safe place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you actually receive wounded persons in the following days and weeks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was on duty twice, in two shifts. The wounded that we were taking in were primarily persons who were ethnic Muslims. I only treated the wounds of a Serb soldier once, a man who was not from Foca. By his accent, I assumed that he was from Serbia. He said, verbatim, "We are going to expel and slaughter all the balijas from Foca." Of course, he did not realise that I was a Muslim. A lot of the wounded were ethnic Muslims. I found this very strange. There was fighting in town. Then as I talked to Dr. Aziz Torlak, I asked him what was going on. He said to me something along these things: that the Serbs had their own field hospitals or something out in the field where they took their wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the wounded Muslims that you received, were they soldiers or were they civilians or both?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: A large number of them were mostly civilians. I saw one man whom Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I supposed to be a military person, and I state that all the rest were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were advised by your boss that you should take your families to the hospital as well. Did you take your family to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I brought my wife and two children, who at the time stayed at a village 4 kilometres away from the hospital. The village was called Karadzic. It was on the Drina River. And on the very day that my boss told us this, I brought my wife and children to the hospital. And most of the other Muslim doctors who happened to be at the hospital did the same. However, the Serbs didn't bring their wives and children to the hospital, and later on it turned out that the day prior to that they had sent their families towards Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Besides the families of the staff members, did other civilians or other Muslims or Serbs or Croats take shelter in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a large number of refugees from the section of the town called Aladza and the section called Donje Polje, even Gornje Polje. They were put in various units, wards. One of them were in the ward which was on the ground floor, and we called that section of the hospital a clinic. Among those people who were mostly civilians, women, elderly, children who fled their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What ethnicity did these people have?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Those were mostly Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did your family stay in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Approximately seven days because a problem emerged in the hospital - there was no food, there was no milk - and I decided to send them back to the village Karadza [phoen] where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the hospital taken over by Serb soldiers while you were there?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that happened on April the 17th in the morning. I woke up -- or rather, I watched from the surgical ward through the window and I saw soldiers in the park in front of the hospital, and it appeared very strange to me. That was the first time that I saw Chetniks. I came out with some nurses who worked with me. I went out into this park, and I wanted to talk to these soldiers. I talked to one of them who happened to be from my village, Josanica, and who in his childhood had left for Serbia. And he told me that he lived in Serbia, but that they had come in to save Serbs from the hands of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you left the hospital approximately at the 20th of April. Why did you leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Because the hospital was not safe any more. Chetniks had their guards around the hospital. One could not leave the hospital without their permission, without the permission of their chief whom they called "Vojvoda." When they occupied the hospital, this Vojvoda held a meeting with the director of the hospital, Sekula Stanic, and the physicians who happened to be there in the hospital. I did not attend that meeting. I was at a neurological ward at the time; however, the hospital became unsafe -- was not safe any more. There were shots heard around the hospital. I had an opportunity to see on the left bank of the Drina River a van that passed with a white flag, and Vojvoda ordered his soldiers to shoot at this van. They started firing from automatic weapons on this van, and this van ended up in the river. We heard the screaming of women, children. We were told that there were wounded, there were dead people there. One of our drivers went to the scene, and I think that he brought back two children, one woman, and one injured man, and told us that one elderly woman was killed on that occasion, a driver, and one child. So I left the hospital because it was not safe there any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Berberkic, you used the term "Chetniks" now several times. What do you mean when you say "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: While talking to this Serb who is -- was from my village but who had left for Serbia, he told me that they were all Chetniks, and their uniforms and the way they acted reminded me of the image of Chetniks during the Second World War. They had these special hats, kokarda signs and they had belts with ammunition. They wore long beards. They had military boots and all the other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So does that mean you refer to Serb soldiers who are dressed in this particular way as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you used -- you mentioned kokarda. What is this? You used the word "kokarda."

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I think that this is an old Serbian emblem that they had on their hats, and I truly do not know the significance, the meaning of it. But I did see that most of the soldiers around the hospital had this emblem on their heads. I believe that an eagle is depicted on this emblem.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were still in the hospital, did you see a person with the name Adnan Isanovic in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I saw him. I even talked to him very briefly. Dr. Torlak was nearby as we talked. Adnan Isanovic was wounded, and it was a shot injury. He was shot through his chest cage. We had to do an x-ray, which we did, and Dr. Torlak, Aziz, said that an urgent surgical intervention was needed in order to drain the blood that gathered in the chest cage. I talked to Adnan very briefly because I was on duty and had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did he come from when he came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where he came from. I have no information to this effect. I don't know whether he came on his own or he was brought there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened to him? Did you actually perform surgery on him?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, surgery was not performed. Later on I heard that some paramilitary formations took him away and another group of wounded persons. They took them behind the hospital and shot them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Adnan Isanovic, who was he? Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I knew him personally. He was an owner of the pizzeria called Amadeus. I frequented this pizzeria, and I believe he was quite a wealthy man. He had a lot of money, and he was well known in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does he have a nickname? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, we called him "Adis." I don't know if he had another nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you left the hospital, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I went to the village to join my family, wife and children, and my parents who lived nearby. The name of this village is Josanica. It is some 4 kilometres away from the hospital on the right bank of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the direction of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is downstream from the hospital towards Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the following days, did you participate in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I had a pistol. I believe it was called a "long 9." I don't know much about weapons, but I was given this pistol by my neighbour Dzano Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you take the weapon, or why did he give it to you?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: I intended to protect myself in case of emergency and one can only shoot one's self with a pistol. You can't do anything else with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this time period, did you observe attacks on Muslim villages in this area around Josanica?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw -- I watched as they attacked, as Chetniks attacked the village called Gornje Paunci, Donja Paunci, Filipovici, when they captured military facilities in Filipovici, and when they attacked Donja Josanica and Gornje Josanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those places that you just mentioned, are these Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: The village is -- the villages on the left bank of the river, Gornje Paunci, Donja Paunci, Filipovici was mostly a Muslim village, whereas the village on the right bank of Drina was a mixed village, Josanica, so it was both a Muslim and a -- both a Muslim and a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see houses in the Muslim villages on the left side of the river burn?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them burn. Since I had binoculars at the time, I was able to see soldiers coming into the houses, setting them on fire, taking out television sets and other equipment. I saw them looting these houses. And I could clearly see soldiers, their uniforms, weapons they carried because the distance of the left and the right bank of the Drina River is not great. So I could clearly see them set houses on fire one by one and set villages on fire one by one as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you said you saw soldiers, what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: AMIR BERBERKIC
utterances.text: Those were the same uniforms as Jovic's Chetniks wore. So the same uniforms with typical hats on their heads, with ammunition belts. I think those were Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's time, and we have to stop here at that point and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly. We will adjourn now and resume at 9.30 in the morning.
